issues.legal_issue: A civil court must refer a disputed tenant-status issue to the tenancy authority when a defendant raises a tenancy claim in a suit to recover agricultural land, and must stay the suit pending that determination.
material_facts: The plaintiff brought a civil suit seeking possession of agricultural land on redemption of a transaction alleged to be a mortgage.
The defendants asserted that the transaction was a lease and that they were protected tenants.
Whether a defendant was a tenant was an issue that arose in the suit.
issues.conclusion: The civil court could entertain the possession suit but could not decide the disputed tenant-status issue. It had to refer that issue to the Mamlatdar and stay the suit pending the Mamlatdar’s decision, then dispose of the suit in light of that decision.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 29, 70(b), and 85 of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, the Mamlatdar has exclusive authority to decide whether a person is a tenant, protected tenant, or permanent tenant, while the civil court may hear a landowner’s suit to recover possession from a trespasser or mortgagee. If the defendant raises a tenancy claim and the issue arises, the civil court must refer it to the Mamlatdar rather than decide it or dismiss the suit outright. Section 85A, introduced while this litigation was pending in the second appeal, provides machinery for that reference. Dhondi Tukaram v. Hari Dadu was approved as correctly stating the law before section 85A; Mudugere Rangaiah v. M. Rangaiah was distinguished, and the Court expressed no view on its correctness.

predicates.civil_suit_to_recover_agricultural_land: A landowner brings a civil suit seeking possession of agricultural land.
predicates.defendant_claims_tenant: A defendant claims to hold the land as a tenant.
predicates.tenant_status_is_in_dispute: The parties dispute whether the defendant has tenant status.

issues.definition: When a civil suit seeks recovery of agricultural land and the defendant claims tenant status that is disputed, the tenancy issue must be referred and the suit stayed.

issues.legal_issue: A higher court hearing a second appeal may set aside an inconsistent finding of the first appellate court even when the opposing party filed no appeal or cross-objections.
material_facts: The first appellate court held that the civil court could not decide whether the defendant was a mortgagee or a tenant, but also confirmed a finding about the amount due on the assumption that the transaction was a mortgage.
The plaintiff appealed to the High Court, and the defendants filed no appeal or cross-objections.

The High Court set aside the finding about the amount due because it was inconsistent with the first appellate court’s conclusion that the civil court could not determine the nature of the transaction.
issues.conclusion: The High Court had jurisdiction to correct the inconsistent finding and set it aside, notwithstanding the absence of an appeal or cross-objections by the defendants.
issues.legal_principle: An appellate court has ample power in a second appeal to correct an error arising from inconsistent findings of the first appellate court. A court that has held it cannot decide an issue cannot also make a finding that depends on deciding that issue; the higher court may set aside that inconsistent finding even without an appeal or cross-objections by the opposing party.

predicates.second_appeal: A party brings a second appeal from a first appellate decision.
predicates.first_appellate_findings_are_inconsisten: The first appellate court makes findings that cannot be reconciled with each other.
predicates.one_finding_depends_on_an_issue_the_cour: A finding relies on deciding an issue that the first appellate court held it lacked authority to decide.
predicates.opposing_party_filed_no_appeal_or_cross_: The opposing party files neither an appeal nor cross-objections challenging the finding.

issues.definition: In a second appeal, if the first appellate court made inconsistent findings and one depends on an issue it declined to decide, the higher court may set aside that finding even if the opposing party filed no appeal or cross-objections.
